passage: Monday. After Class 10 results, Darshan felt pulled three ways: Science, Commerce, Humanities. "Everyone has an opinion and nobody has a method," he told Mridul. Mridul shrugged. "So make one." Wednesday. Darshan drew a table. Down the side: what he enjoys, family support, cost, career options, marks trend. Across the top: the three streams. He scored each from one to five, then gave enjoyment and marks trend double weight. Saturday. Totals: Commerce 31, Science 29, Humanities 24. The gap surprised him: Science had won his heart but not his marks trend. He showed the table to his parents. They did not agree with every number, but for the first time they argued about numbers instead of feelings.

passage: Sudha, you look lost with those stream forms. Your Zainab Phuppo was lost too, after Class 10. Science, Commerce or Humanities, and everyone had an opinion. So one night I took a sheet of Abba's ledger paper and drew a grid. Down the side: interest, how my marks had been going, jobs it could lead to, cost, and whether the family would back it. Across the top, the three streams. I gave each box a score out of five. Then I thought, these don't matter equally. Interest counts double, because I'll be living with it for two years. Cost counts too, because Abba was paying. When I added it all up, Humanities came first, Commerce close behind, Science last, though everyone expected Science. The grid didn't decide for me. It showed me what I was trading.

qa.q: What did young Zainab draw the grid on?
qa.a: A sheet of Abba's ledger paper.

qa.q: Why did young Zainab make interest count double?
qa.a: Young Zainab felt that enjoying the subject mattered most and was probably anxious about spending two years on something she didn't care for.

qa.q: Which step inside the story made the trade-offs clear, and why?
qa.a: Weighting the rows, like doubling interest, because it showed which factors mattered most instead of treating every box as equal.

qa.q: How might Abba have felt when Humanities came out on top?
qa.a: Abba may have been surprised, since everyone expected Science, but seeing the reasoning on paper could make it easier to support.

grounding: An elder recalls scoring three streams on weighted factors after Class 10 so the trade-offs became visible.

passage: The stream-choice form was due at school on Monday, and it was already Saturday night. Lalit's father wanted Science, his mother thought Commerce was safer, and Lalit himself kept drifting toward History books. His cousin Chaitanya, visiting from Pune, pulled out a notebook. "Stop arguing in your head. Score them." They made columns for Science, Commerce and Humanities, and rows for interest, how his marks had moved over two years, careers, coaching costs and family support. Lalit scored each from one to five. "Now, which rows matter most to you?" Lalit thought. "Interest. And careers." They doubled those. Science won on family support, Humanities on interest by a mile, Commerce sat in the middle. Totals: Humanities 29, Commerce 26, Science 24. Lalit looked at the gap for a long time. "So it's not just a feeling. There's a real difference."

qa.q: When was the stream-choice form due?
qa.a: It was due at school on Monday.

qa.q: How does Lalit seem to feel looking at the totals?
qa.a: He seems surprised and a bit relieved that his pull toward Humanities shows up as a real difference, not just a feeling.

qa.q: What could Lalit do next with the grid?
qa.a: Show it to his parents, so they can all see the trade-offs, including the low family-support score, and talk them through together.

qa.q: How might Lalit's father see the totals?
qa.a: His father may feel disappointed that Science came last, but the scores give a clear starting point for talking instead of arguing.

grounding: Shows a student, under deadline, weighting and scoring three streams so the trade-offs become visible rather than vague.
